Thyroid

Normal TSH, but Still Feel Hypothyroid?

By Adam Seay, D.C., Root Health, Garner, NC. Updated October 2, 2026.

The short answer

A TSH is a screening test. It shows what your pituitary gland thinks of your thyroid hormone level, not what your cells are actually getting. Hashimoto's can run for years with a TSH inside the normal range, and low free T3 can leave you feeling hypothyroid while TSH and free T4 both look fine. If you are tired, cold, foggy and stuck on weight with a normal result, the next step is a fuller panel.

What TSH actually tells you

TSH, thyroid stimulating hormone, comes from the pituitary gland at the base of your brain. When the pituitary senses too little thyroid hormone in your blood, it pushes TSH up to tell the thyroid to work harder. That makes TSH a useful first look. It is also an indirect one. It measures the signal, not the result.

The conventional reference range runs roughly 0.4 to 4.5 mIU/L. When someone has symptoms, I work toward a tighter target of 1.0 to 2.5. That target is a clinical guide for deciding what to investigate next, not a validated cutoff for a diagnosis, and you deserve to know the difference.

Three things a TSH alone can miss

1. Hashimoto's in its early years

Hashimoto's thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in developed countries.1 It is an immune problem first: the immune system makes antibodies against thyroid tissue and slowly wears the gland down. That process can be active for years, sometimes decades, before TSH climbs above the cutoff. During that window, a TSH-only test reads normal.

Two antibody tests, TPO antibodies and thyroglobulin antibodies, show whether that immune process is there. Positive antibodies alongside a normal TSH also mean a higher chance of becoming hypothyroid later, which is a good reason to keep checking. What antibodies are not is a scoreboard. Lowering the number has not been shown to make anyone feel better, so I use them to establish what is going on and to monitor it, not as the goal.

2. Conversion from T4 to T3

Your thyroid mostly makes T4, which is inactive. Your body has to convert it to T3, the form that acts on nearly every cell. That conversion depends on selenium, zinc, decent liver function and a low inflammatory load. When conversion is poor, free T3 runs low while TSH and free T4 look normal, and you can feel every symptom of an underactive thyroid.

3. Stress and reverse T3

Under chronic stress or inflammation, more T4 gets turned into reverse T3, an inactive form that competes with active T3. Cortisol, the main stress hormone, also suppresses the enzyme that converts T4 into active T3.2 That is one reason long stretches of stress and thyroid type fatigue so often travel together. The ratio of free T3 to reverse T3 is one of the more useful numbers in a full panel.

Subclinical hypothyroidism, a raised TSH with normal thyroid hormone levels, affects up to one in ten adults, and many people with it report fatigue, foggy thinking and low mood.3 Being told a result is "only borderline" is not the same as being told nothing is there.

The panel worth asking for

If your symptoms do not match your "normal" result, these are the tests I want to see together:

  • TSH, free T4 and free T3, drawn together, so conversion can be judged.
  • Reverse T3, to see whether stress or inflammation is pulling T4 away from the active form.
  • TPO and thyroglobulin antibodies, to find out whether this is Hashimoto's.
  • Ferritin, B12 and vitamin D. Low iron stores alone can cause fatigue. In one randomized trial, women with a ferritin under 50 and no anemia saw fatigue drop about 48 percent on iron compared with 29 percent on placebo.4 Plenty of labs still call a ferritin under 50 normal.

Ask your own physician first. When they will run these, it is usually the cheaper route. If you have already been told everything is fine and would rather not wait, many of the panels I use can be ordered directly through my patient portal. Ordering a test and knowing what to do with the result are two different things, so bring the results to your physician or to me before acting on them.

What not to do with a normal TSH

  • Do not change or stop any thyroid medication on your own. Dose decisions belong to you and your prescriber.
  • Do not start iodine on a hunch. When iodine is used in Hashimoto's, it should be a deliberate decision, paired with selenium and monitored.
  • Do not judge progress by an antibody number. Judge it by energy, clear thinking, sleep, hair, how you handle the cold and how you feel by mid-afternoon.

Common questions

Can you have Hashimoto's with a normal TSH?

Yes. The immune process behind Hashimoto's can be active for years before TSH rises out of range. TPO and thyroglobulin antibodies are the tests that show it.

Is free T3 part of a standard thyroid test?

Usually not. Many routine checkups run TSH alone, sometimes with free T4. Free T3 and reverse T3 normally have to be asked for.

I already take thyroid medication and still feel tired. Is this the same problem?

Partly. Still tired on levothyroxine? covers absorption, iron, celiac testing and the other things worth checking once you are already treated.
